OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: Cheap Talk, Real Stakes: Commitment and Exploitation in Human-LLM Strategic Interaction
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: LLM agents now negotiate, allocate resources, and make commitments on a user's behalf. The vulnerability is not only in the final move but in what comes before it: in pre-action conversation, a model can be primed to make promises, lock in commitments, or reveal intentions that a counterpart will exploit when the action is finally taken. Yet standard game-based evaluations usually observe only the final move, leaving the speech-action gap unmeasured. We study this gap directly by introducing HL-PACT, a controlled platform with matched human-human, human-LLM, and LLM-LLM sessions across five repeated games: Prisoner's Dilemma, Battle of the Sexes, Ultimatum, Kuhn Poker, and Liar's Dice. Across 3,553 sessions, we randomize free-form pre-round chat and opponent identity masking, classify each message by its strategic content, and compare what players say, how they say it, and when the two diverge. We find that LLMs consistently activate the communication channel: mixed pairs contain more proposals, promises, and strategic reasoning than human pairs, with humans adapting to the LLM's negotiation register. This improves equilibrium selection in coordination games and shifts bargaining toward fairer offers. In games with profitable unilateral deviation, however, the same communication structure can create asymmetries: when identity is known, human partners selectively adapt to LLMs’ willingness to follow through on stated intentions, producing measurable exploitation. Masking reduces this asymmetry and makes the communication benefit more symmetric. The strategic value of language therefore depends on game structure, counterpart identity, and whether speech is separated from action. Evaluating LLM agents without communication can miss a central deployment risk: models may not fail because they reason poorly, but because their reliability is predictable.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: Gravity-Bench-v1: A Benchmark on Gravitational Physics Discovery for Agents
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Modern science emerged from reasoning over repeatedly-observed planetary motions. We present Gravity-Bench-v1, an environment-based benchmark that challenges AI agents on tasks that parallel this historical development. Gravity-Bench-v1 evaluates agents on the discovery of physics concealed within a dynamic environment, using rigorous gravitational dynamics simulations. Gravity-Bench includes out-of-distribution cases, i.e. with physics that deviates from the real world, to evaluate true scientific generalization capabilities. Agents must plan to collect data within an experimental budget and must perform a dynamic form of data analysis and reasoning to solve tasks efficiently. Our benchmark admits an open-ended space of solutions. Reference solutions for each task are provided to calibrate AI performance against human expertise. Technically at an upper-undergraduate level, our benchmark proves challenging to baseline AI agents. Gravity-Bench-v1 and planned extensions should help map out AI progress towards scientific discovery capabilities.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.05572.title: Disentangling Task Difficulty from Run-Level Failure in Agent Failure Prediction
arXiv|arxiv:2610.05572.abstract: Predicting whether an LLM agent will fail has emerged as a promising direction for supporting intervention during execution. Recent approaches report strong predictive performance, often with AUROC values between 0.85 and 0.94. However, predictors are typically trained by pooling runs from many tasks. We hypothesize that part of this performance comes from recognizing that some tasks are harder than others, rather than detecting whether a particular run is heading toward failure. This distinction matters because task-level difficulty supports decisions about where to allocate computation, while run-level prediction is needed to decide whether to intervene in an ongoing trajectory. We study benchmarks with repeated attempts of the same task by the same agent and separate cross-unit comparisons from comparisons between successful and failed runs of the same model-task unit. Across the evaluated corpora, more than 99.93% of the positive-negative pairs underlying pooled AUROC are cross-unit. Accordingly, predictors that never observe the current run can achieve high pooled performance, including a difficulty oracle with AUROC up to 0.945, while remaining at chance within task. Early run-level discrimination is consistently weak across trajectory predictors, released monitors, and hidden-state probes, although it improves later in execution and is stronger for weaker agents. Under fixed token budgets, task-level allocation outperforms abort-only strategies, while early stopping becomes beneficial only when within-task AUROC reaches about 0.84-0.93, far above the 0.50-0.55 range observed for early monitors. These results show that failure prediction should be evaluated not only by outcome accuracy, but by whether the captured signal supports the intended deployment decision.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.39220.title: Learning Process Rewards via Reasoning State Propagation
arXiv|arxiv:2609.39220.abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) have demonstrated notable effectiveness in test-time scaling and reinforcement learning by providing fine-grained signals for evaluating intermediate reasoning states, but their training relies heavily on costly process annotations. A natural way to alleviate this dependence is to complement limited process supervision with scalable outcome supervision. However, existing PRMs often model reasoning prefixes independently, providing no explicit mechanism for effectively using final outcome to guide the learning of intermediate reasoning states. We introduce Reasoning State Propagation (RSP), which represents each reasoning prefix with a binary validity state and models transitions between successive states across the reasoning trajectory. Specifically, RSP predicts a break probability that a valid state becomes invalid and a repair probability that an invalid state returns to valid. By propagating these transitions, RSP connects intermediate states to the final state, allowing process annotations to supervise intermediate states while outcome labels supervise the final state and can provide learning signals to preceding steps. Across reasoning search, response selection, and reinforcement learning, RSP consistently outperforms representative PRM baselines, with average improvements over Qwen2.5-Math-PRM of 5.6% in beam search and 2.1% in reinforcement learning.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.01027.title: LawCompass: Navigating from Legal QA to Multi-Agent Deep Research with Grounded Evidence
arXiv|arxiv:2610.01027.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) have significantly democratized access to legal information. Nevertheless, most existing legal assistants remain confined to multi-turn conversational QA, failing to support complex legal tasks that require systematic evidence retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and report-level synthesis. In this paper, we present LawCompass, an evidence-grounded legal assistant that navigates the transition from standard Legal QA to multi-agent deep research. LawCompass provides three task-oriented functions: Legal QA, which delivers precise, evidence-backed answers to legal questions; Professional Retrieval, which enables structured exploration of statutes and judicial cases via query rewriting; and Deep Research, which employs a multi-agent workflow to decompose complex legal tasks and synthesize comprehensive research reports. Crucially, LawCompass maintains explicit citation links across all modules, empowering users to directly verify system outputs against original legal sources. Evaluation results demonstrate that LawCompass provides a practical and scalable paradigm for transforming conversational AI into trustworthy and evidence-grounded legal research assistance.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.15563.title: Anticipatory Textile MMG-Strain Sensing for Confirm-Then-Assist Soft Knee Exosuits
arXiv|arxiv:2610.15563.abstract: Soft wearable robots must commit to assistance around movement onset, when the available signals are ambiguous. Surface electromyography (sEMG) detects neuromuscular drive early but degrades under sweat and electrode shift, and kinematic sensors respond only once the limb moves. This letter presents a knitted textile interface that co-samples a three-channel mechanomyography (MMG) array and an anterior strain sensor on a single synchronous 500 Hz clock. Across five participants, MMG activation preceded strain-detected knee motion during sit-to-stand by per-channel medians of 322-344 ms. Sampled on the same clock, the sign of the strain slope resolved movement direction on 649 of 650 completed transitions with no training or per-participant calibration, raising four-class balanced accuracy from 90.3% to 95.6%. The fused signals drove a two-stage confirm-then-assist policy for a soft pneumatic knee. Across 240 trials in four participants, the onboard controller entered the assist state on 78 of 80 sit-to-stand trials and on none of the 80 isometric co-contractions. It also entered the assist state on 27 of 80 stand-to-sit trials and left it at the hold timeout, motivating an antagonistic flexor gauge to resolve this direction at onset. Co-sampling muscle acoustics with textile strain on one clock lets the inflation command be issued around movement onset.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.41260.title: SketchDirector: Complex Scene Sketching via Agentic Layout Reasoning and Detail Refinement
arXiv|arxiv:2610.41260.abstract: Existing sketch generation methods often rely on image guidance and are largely limited to individual objects or simplified scenes, leaving text-guided complex scene sketching underexplored. We present SketchDirector, an agentic framework that mimics the human sketching workflow for automatic multi-concept scene sketching. Given a scene-level text prompt, SketchDirector first employs a large language model~(LLM) to decompose the scene into multiple draft assets, where each is represented by a set of Bézier curves. Then, an agentic reasoning loop iteratively plans and executes their spatial arrangement, guided by self-evolving memory. Finally, a detail refinement module leverages diffusion priors to enhance sketch quality while preserving geometric structure. To support future research and applications in multi-concept scene sketch generation, we further introduce the MCSketch8K dataset, comprising editable vector assets, compositional layouts, and object-level manipulation annotations. Extensive experiments show that SketchDirector outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in semantic and compositional quality while effectively preserving overall contour organization during refinement.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.31559.title: COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation
arXiv|arxiv:2611.31559.abstract: LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. COGENT draws on established cognitive theories, such as Norman's action cycle and ACT-R, to enable explainable, intervenable, and modular user simulation by decomposing the simulation process into cognitive modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. We begin by presenting six intervenability demonstrations, each tracing how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a processing module propagates through the cognitive pipeline to produce a behavioral change. We evaluate COGENT's behavioral and attributional fidelity across three benchmarks -- AgentNetBench, A11y-CUA, and SENSE-42 -- finding that it achieves statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior and recovers the relational structure among human self-reported psychological states. Together, these demos and evaluations demonstrate COGENT's utility toward more faithful, explainable, intervenable, and modular LLM-based cognitive simulations.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.18614.title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2610.18614.abstract: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. We propose a method to calibrate it against the eventual outcome of a multi-step episode: under GRPO, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule scores each step's confidence against the realized outcome. In offline RL on recorded trajectories of a Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop environments, the AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85, and the top-10% of steps the agent is most confident about succeed ~4.3x more often than average. In online RL on the live ALFWorld agent, four calibration rewards improve early-step AUROC, expected calibration error goes from 0.42 to below 0.12, and selective execution improves over both the untrained agent and a format-only RL control, without degrading task success. We also introduce an evaluation protocol that separates episode depth, task difficulty, and attempt-level foresight, which shows where the gain lies: the trained agent recognizes from its first step which tasks it will fail, while telling a succeeding attempt from a failing one at the same task is harder, with some early-window signal emerging on TextWorld.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.36478.title: Learning to Harvest Without Collapse in a Regenerative Commons: A Lagrangian Framework
arXiv|arxiv:2609.36478.abstract: The tragedy of the commons poses a multi-agent safety problem: reward-seeking agents can deplete a shared resource, and cooperation among its users does not itself specify how much must be preserved. We make preservation an explicit requirement by formulating a regenerative commons as a constrained Markov game or a constrained multi-agent MDP with a designer-specified depletion budget. We develop a nonstationary Lagrangian framework that constructs a policy sequence from solutions of unconstrained games or cooperative control problems. Extending earlier time-average constructions, we introduce average-epoch solution concepts for reset episodes with discounted rewards and terminal costs. We prove a reward-independent feasibility certificate, cooperative feasibility and approximate optimality against feasible policy mixtures, and an extension to unbiased sampled costs. For self-interested agents, a constrained Nash certificate quantifies the price-dispersion term introduced by deviations that redistribute budget across epochs. Under the stated assumptions on solver accuracy and multiplier updates, these results give constrained policy-sequence guarantees using solutions of unconstrained problems. Experiments with constrained IPPO and MAPPO in a Gordon-Schaefer fishery examine how depletion budgets shape stock retention, harvest rewards, and price adaptation.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.08219.title: Agent-R$^2$: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis
arXiv|arxiv:2611.08219.abstract: Large language models have made rapid progress in agentic reasoning and tool use, raising expectations for agents that can take over realistic productivity work from humans. However, current agents still struggle to finish such tasks, where success requires following long-horizon professional workflows, understanding heterogeneous file contexts, and producing usable deliverables under fine-grained requirements. A key bottleneck is the lack of scalable post-training data that reflects real work intent, authentic file environments, and deliverable-level evaluation. To close this gap, we introduce Agent-R$^2$, a $\textbf{r}$eal-source data synthesis framework that scales training data for $\textbf{r}$ealistic productivity work. Instead of relying on manually specified workflows or LLM-generated files, Agent-R$^2$ grounds synthesis throughout the pipeline in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and authentic web-sourced files. From 10k web-corpus candidates, Agent-R$^2$ distills 4k task instances that pair real multi-format attachments with fine-grained, deliverable-level rubrics. On this data, we train Agent-R$^2$-4B via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning, improving both end-to-end productivity performance and file-grounded reasoning. Trained on only 4k instances, Agent-R$^2$-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on both GDPval (51.0$\%$ vs. 48.0$\%$) and OfficeQA (14.8$\%$ vs. 13.8$\%$). Further analysis shows that Agent-R$^2$ mitigates shortcut behavior, where agents produce superficially plausible deliverables before sufficiently grounding, constructing, or verifying them, while promoting sustained exploration.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.09684.title: From Pareto to Preference: Personalized Test-Time Scaling via Amortized Agentic Policy Discovery
arXiv|arxiv:2610.09684.abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models by allocating additional inference computation. arXiv|arxiv:2509.16886.title: SAM-DCE: Decoupled Context Enhancement for Prompt-Free Medical Image Segmentation
arXiv|arxiv:2509.16886.abstract: The Segment Anything Model (SAM) is a promising foundation model for medical image segmentation, but its prompt-driven design is not directly suitable for fully automatic multi-class anatomical segmentation. arXiv|arxiv:2611.32624.title: HiCal: Offline Calibration for Hierarchical Scale Encoding in Accurate HiF4 Quantization
arXiv|arxiv:2611.32624.abstract: Block floating-point (BFP) quantization is widely adopted for efficient low-bit large language model (LLM) inference, where the choice of block scales plays a critical role in quantization accuracy. HiFloat4 (HiF4) employs a hierarchical scale encoding scheme consisting of a global E6M2 scale and two levels of binary scale extensions. However, its conventional rounding rule and fixed scale extension thresholds may not fully capture the statistical characteristics of the quantized tensors in practice, leading to suboptimal scale representations. Specifically, we introduce a calibrated rounding bias for the Level-1 E6M2 scale and optimize the scale-extension thresholds at Levels 2 and 3 based on the empirical distributions of local group magnitudes. The resulting calibration parameters are determined offline and remain fixed during inference, while the hierarchical encoding continues to adapt to individual blocks through their local values. This design eliminates the need for per-block multi-candidate scale search while preserving the original deterministic HiF4 encoding procedure. Experiments across five synthetic and real activation distributions show that the proposed method reduces quantization MSE by 9.91%-23.50% relative to the original HiF4 scheme, including a 13.00% reduction on real Qwen3-8B activations. End-to-end evaluations across six benchmarks further show average-score improvements of 0.91 and 1.25 percentage points on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, respectively, without per-block multi-candidate search during inference.

arXiv|arxiv:2509.09906.title: Towards using Large Language Models for Risk Negotiation and Consensus-building in One Health contexts
arXiv|arxiv:2509.09906.abstract: Risk negotiation under the One Health framework requires balancing competing stakeholder interests across human, animal, and environmental health domains - a process constrained by information complexity and time pressure. This study presents and evaluates a multi-step pipeline that integrates large language model-based agents into a human-supervised negotiation process, specifically targeting risk assessment, valuation, and negotiation steps. Agent descriptions were generated from stakeholder-provided materials using retrieval-augmented generation methods. During preliminary multi-agent discussions, agents accessed domain-specific computational models and web-based sources before human participants refined proposed issues and options. A simulated negotiation game then produced distributions of candidate deals, characterised using Nash bargaining solution criteria and Pareto optimality metrics. The developed approach was evaluated in a workshop involving independent domain experts across two real-world scenarios: food safety criteria for Campylobacter in broiler meat and oak processionary moth management. In this feasibility evaluation, participants reached consensus with the allotted time after discussing and modifying the proposed deals. The framework offers an adaptable blueprint for AI-assisted risk negotiation; the specific contribution of LLM assistance, including gains in efficiency and decision quality, requires comparative evaluation.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.26221.title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
arXiv|arxiv:2611.26221.abstract: Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming language (NL/PL). To follow data across it, an analysis needs a data-flow summary of which placeholders the output uses, but no code describes what the model does. Analyses of these LLM-integrated applications therefore taint every output with every input, creating spurious flows, or ask a second model to label each call, which is costly. We prove, and mechanize in Lean 4, that a placeholder flows to the output of a transformer, to first order, only through the attention that reads it (no reading, no flow), and that a faint reading or sensitivity cannot certify that a placeholder does not flow. Unlike reading, the log-probability gradients and Fisher signals of existing methods vanish on confident outputs, and single-span removal fails on duplicated content. Our tool, Sightline, reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which reads are uses, and calibrates the pruning to miss at most a chosen fraction $α$ of true flows, on average over call sites, when deployment is exchangeable with calibration. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, Sightline is the most accurate summary against the seven closest methods and a hidden-state probe. Calibrated at $α$ = 1%, it misses about 1% of true flows and prunes 43.9-65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the best baseline, and still 43.8-60.1% when calibrated on another collection. Through an open surrogate, it reads models treated as closed about as accurately as they read themselves, without their labels. In the information-flow control of an LLM agent, it removes about half of the labels from inputs that do not flow.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.32424.title: CyberClear: A Benchmark for LLM Agent Systems on APT Attack Chain Provenance
arXiv|arxiv:2609.32424.abstract: Large language model agents have demonstrated promising capabilities in cybersecurity tasks, yet their ability to reconstruct complete Advanced Persistent Threat attack campaigns from complex security logs remains largely unexplored. Existing cybersecurity benchmarks for agents mainly focus on vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and security analysis tasks, leaving the evaluation of attack chain provenance under realistic security logs insufficiently studied. To address this gap, we introduce CyberClear, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents and advanced agent systems on APT attack chain provenance from long-context security logs. CyberClear covers both single-step attacks and multi-stage attack chains, requiring agents to identify attack evidence, infer attack progression, and generate provenance graphs containing entities, causal relationships, MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and forensic evidence. To enable comprehensive evaluation, we develop an evaluation method tailored to APT attack chain provenance. Unlike conventional text similarity metrics that focus on surface-level matching, our evaluation examines whether reconstructed graphs preserve the semantics of attack chains across single-step behavior correctness, multi-step behavior identification, temporal and causal consistency, entity and relationship fidelity, and overall attack narrative consistency. Advanced multi-agent systems powered by state-of-the-art LLMs still struggle on CyberClear, motivating us to propose CyberProvenance, an agent cyber harness designed for multi-agents that augments LLM agents with evidence accumulation, execution-based validation, and feedback-guided refinement mechanisms for reliable attack-chain provenance. Extensive evaluations on CyberClear demonstrate the effectiveness of CyberProvenance in improving evidence reasoning, execution-grounded validation, and complete APT attack chain reconstruction.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: On the Entropy Calibration of Language Models
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: We study the problem of entropy calibration, which asks whether a language model's entropy over generations matches its log loss on human text. Past work found that models are miscalibrated, with entropy per step increasing as generations grow longer, due to error accumulation. To calibrate the model and improve text quality, it has become standard practice to truncate the distribution, but this approach reduces output diversity, which we would like to avoid. Therefore, in this paper, we ask: does miscalibration improve automatically with scale, and if not, is it theoretically possible to calibrate without tradeoffs? To build intuition, we first study a simplified theoretical setting to characterize the scaling behavior of miscalibration with respect to dataset size. We find that the rate of scaling depends on the power law exponent of the data distribution --- in particular, for a power law exponent close to 1, the scaling exponent is close to 0, meaning that miscalibration improves very slowly with scale. Next, we measure miscalibration empirically in language models ranging from 0.5B to 70B parameters. We find that the observed scaling behavior is similar to what is predicted theoretically: our fitted scaling exponents for text are close to 0, meaning that larger models accumulate error at a similar rate as smaller ones. This scaling (or, lack thereof) provides one explanation for why we sample from larger models with similar amounts of truncation as smaller models, even though the larger models are of higher quality. However, truncation is not a satisfying solution because it comes at the cost of increased log loss. In theory, is it even possible to reduce entropy while preserving log loss? We prove that it is possible, if we assume access to a black box which can fit models to predict the future entropy of text.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: From Player to Master: Enhancing Test-Time Learning of LLM Agents via Reinforcement Learning over Memory
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in long-running settings where improving through experience at test time becomes important. A common approach is to update an explicit memory after each interaction to guide future decisions. However, most existing methods rely on hand-designed prompting rules, making it difficult to align memory updates with downstream objectives over multi-step horizons consistently. We propose MemoPilot, a plug-in memory copilot that explicitly trains the memory update process to improve a frozen LLM's performance across sequential interactions. We formulate memory updating as a multi-turn decision problem and optimize it end-to-end with multi-turn GRPO. Our training recipe introduces (i) a turn-wise reward signal and (ii) a context-independent, turn-level advantage estimation across rollouts, enabling finer-grained credit assignment and more stable training in multi-turn settings. We evaluate MemoPilot on two testbeds: multi-round Rock-Paper-Scissors (RPS) and Limit Texas Hold'em (LHE). Across both environments, MemoPilot substantially improves test-time learning of a frozen player over strong baselines, ranking first in Elo ratings on both games (1762 on LHE and 1590 on RPS) and outperforming all baseline memory methods and proprietary models, including Deepseek-V3.2. Our code is publicly available.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.22226.title: Swiss-Knife: A Framework for Reconfigurable Externalised Multi-Objective Alignment at Decode Time
arXiv|arxiv:2609.22226.abstract: Decode-time alignment methods steer a frozen language model by scoring candidate continuations with an external reward and selecting the maximiser. We argue that this shared design is a single degenerate point in a much larger space. We introduce Swiss-Knife, a framework for externalised multi-objective alignment in which the alignment specification is a first-class runtime object: hot-swappable scoring blades, a batch normaliser, a pairwise aggregation operator, and a selection rule. Six axioms characterise the admissible aggregation operators, and we prove a representation theorem: every operator satisfying them has the form $R_i = \sum_{j \neq i} g((μ_i - μ_j)/s(σ_i,σ_j))$, a two-parameter family containing probit and logistic comparison rules and pointwise argmax as named coordinates. Within it, pairwise aggregation is Lipschitz-stable under adversarial reward contamination while argmax is not, and Candidate-Batch Normalization (CBN) makes the weight simplex invariant to the rescalings under which reward models are only ever identified. Our reference instantiation pairs DPO-LoRA blades with an uncertainty-aware pairwise tournament. Sweeping the helpfulness/honesty/harmlessness simplex, it attains the best balanced frontier of six decode-time methods (harmonic $F_1$ 0.797 vs. 0.750 for the strongest baseline, $p < 10^{-14}$) with the lowest refusal rate and highest helpfulness of any arm, and reconfigures its objectives in 0.05 ms with no gradient computation.

arXiv|arxiv:2605.05794.title: MoLS: SNR-Guided Module-Wise Learning-Rate Calibration for Large Language Models
arXiv|arxiv:2605.05794.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) contain functionally distinct modules with heterogeneous gradient statistics. Although Adam(W) adapts updates at the parameter level, selecting relative learning rates across modules often relies on costly manual tuning. We study this problem through gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Our analysis identifies structural sources of module-wise SNR differences and relates SNR to the attenuation of Adam's normalized mean-gradient component. Based on these findings, we propose \textbf{Module-wise Learning Rate Scaling via SNR (\name)}, a lightweight method that replaces manual multiplier search with one-shot calibration. MoLS estimates module-level SNRs after an initial adaptation period and uses inverse-square-root scaling to determine relative learning-rate multipliers. The multipliers are introduced smoothly during warmup and then held fixed while the global learning-rate schedule continues. Our theoretical results quantify the effect of calibration and its sensitivity to estimation error and relative SNR drift. Extensive experiments across LLM pre-training and fine-tuning show that MoLS reduces perplexity and improves downstream accuracy with minimal computational overhead. It achieves performance comparable to carefully tuned module-specific learning rates and integrates with memory-efficient optimizers and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.08954.title: RACER: Reflective Agent Coupling Query Interpretation and Tool-Based Retrieval for Frame Selection in Long Video Understanding
arXiv|arxiv:2610.08954.abstract: Video large language models (Vid-LLMs) excel at diverse video-language tasks by reasoning over selected frames. However, frame selection for long videos remains challenging, as it requires retrieving relevant frames distributed across segments from a large candidate pool given complex queries. This paper investigates dominant approaches to long-video frame selection from a task-decomposition perspective, identifying two key challenges: the Query Comprehension Gap in similarity-based methods and the Interpretation--Selection Gap in judgment-based methods. To address them, we propose RACER, a training-free reflective agentic framework that decomposes long-video frame selection into query interpretation driven by a lightweight Vid-LLM and evidence localization supported by an embedding model serving as a retrieval tool. Specifically, the Vid-LLM is responsible solely for reformulating the complex query into sub-queries that make implicit information requirements explicit, mitigating the Query Comprehension Gap. Meanwhile, the retrieval tool leverages these sub-queries to localize relevant evidence, relieving the Vid-LLM of direct frame selection and thus addressing the Interpretation--Selection Gap. Finally, the retrieved frames are fed back to the Vid-LLM for sub-query refinement, forming a reflection loop that iteratively improves query interpretation and frame selection. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show that RACER consistently improves long video understanding. Notably, RACER achieves effective frame selection even with limited-capability components, demonstrating that agentic integration enables these components to enhance more capable Vid-LLMs.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.24532.title: Contrastive Hypergraph Source-free Domain Adaptive Object Detection in Adverse Weather Conditions--Extended Version
arXiv|arxiv:2610.24532.abstract: Adverse weather conditions such as fog, rain, snow, and low illumination introduce structured visibility degradations that severely impair object detectors trained on clear-weather data. When source data are inaccessible due to privacy or trans- mission constraints, source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) becomes necessary. However, existing SFDA methods based on pairwise contrastive learning struggle to capture high-order semantics and often suffer from agreement collapse under severe corruption. We propose REUNION, a hypergraph-guided SFDA framework for object detection in adverse weather conditions. REUNION constructs a contrastive hypergraph over target-domain object proposals, encoding high-order relations through intra-image context, weather-aware grouping, prototype-based semantic anchors, and uncertainty-aware connections between reliable and low-confidence instances. To effectively exploit these structured relations, we introduce a group-wise Hyper-InfoNCE objective that optimizes representations at the hyperedge level, enabling semantic information to propagate from confident proposals to corrupted or low-contrast instances. Experiments with diverse benchmarks demonstrate that REUNION effectively mitigates domain shifts and achieves state-of-the-art performance in SFDA settings.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.37882.title: FYC: FPR-Disparity Weight Perturbation and Youden Calibration for Fair Deepfake Detection
arXiv|arxiv:2610.37882.abstract: Deepfake detectors routinely achieve high aggregate accuracy while exhibiting substantial demographic disparities in their errors: false-positive rates differ by double digits across gender and skin tone. Most existing remedies require either full retraining with a fairness-aware objective or demographic-annotated training data, both impractical when only a pretrained checkpoint is available, while label-free post-hoc calibrators leave the detector's weights unchanged. We introduce FYC (FPR-disparity Weight Perturbation and Youden Calibration), a two-stage post-hoc method that perturbs a detector's weights under an FPR-disparity criterion, then calibrates a separate decision threshold for each demographic group - requiring no architectural changes and no full retraining. Evaluated against every detector benchmarked on AI-Face v2 across six intersectional gender x skin-tone groups, FYC outperforms the field on 18 of 21 reported fairness and utility metrics, including purpose-built fairness architectures, at a fraction of the training cost. We further identify why the choice of fairness criterion is critical: the original Demographic Parity objective used in prior weight-perturbation work is architecture-dependent and unpredictable, improving two of four evaluated architectures, leaving a third largely unchanged, and substantially degrading the fourth (PG-FDD), with no way to anticipate the outcome for a given checkpoint in advance. Conditioning the same objective on real images only - our FPR-disparity criterion - eliminates this unpredictability, improving fairness and accuracy jointly across all four architectures with no exceptions.

arXiv|arxiv:2607.10103.title: LLM Watermarking as Big Data Provenance: A Deployment-Oriented Systematization
arXiv|arxiv:2607.10103.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) generate and transform content at scale, reliable attribution becomes an increasingly important requirement for big data provenance. Although numerous watermarking methods have been proposed, existing evaluations predominantly emphasize sample-level detectability and robustness, leaving deployment requirements such as serving efficiency, population-scale false positives, multi-key attribution, and long-term verification less systematically examined. This paper presents a deployment-oriented systematization of LLM watermarking through the five Vs of big data: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, and Value. We classify representative watermarking methods across four dimensions: insertion point, verification authority, operational state, and adversarial threat model. We further map these methods to four deployment workloads: online generation, streaming detection, transformation pipelines, and ecosystem governance. Our synthesis identifies recurring limitations, including dependencies on generation-time access, additional inference overhead, sensitivity to downstream transformations, and incomplete reporting of calibration and lifecycle compatibility. Based on these findings, we propose workload-specific evaluation requirements covering statistical reliability, throughput, utility, robustness, and governance. This framework connects watermark design choices to practical deployment constraints and provides guidance for selecting and evaluating provenance mechanisms in large-scale data ecosystems.

ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.title: Do LLMs Know Tool Irrelevance? Demystifying Structural Alignment Bias in Tool Invocations
ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in utilizing external tools. In practice, however, LLMs are often exposed to tools that are irrelevant to the user’s query, in which case the desired behavior is to refrain from invocations. In this work, we identify a widespread yet overlooked mechanistic flaw in tool refusal, which we term structural alignment bias: Even when a tool fails to serve the user’s goal, LLMs still tend to invoke it whenever query attributes can be validly assigned to tool parameters. To systematically study this bias, we introduce SABEval, a new dataset that decouples structural alignment from semantic relevance. Our analysis shows that structural alignment bias induces severe tool-invocation errors in LLMs, yet remains largely unaccounted for in existing evaluations. To investigate the internal mechanisms underlying this bias, we propose Contrastive Attention Attribution, which reveals two competing pathways for semantic checking and structural matching. The relative strength of these pathways drives LLMs’ tool invocation decisions. Based on these findings, we further introduce a rebalancing strategy that effectively mitigates structural alignment bias, as demonstrated by extensive experiments, without degrading general tool-use capabilities.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.18790.title: EqC: Equilibrium Energy Control for Introspective Lifelong Robot Learning
arXiv|arxiv:2610.18790.abstract: Long-term robot autonomy depends on more than effective action generation: a policy must recognize when its behavior is no longer sufficiently supported and use assistance to improve. We introduce Equilibrium Energy Control (EqC), a framework for introspective lifelong robot learning built around an explicit conditional energy landscape. EqC casts generative action refinement as equilibrium-seeking optimization, while the geometry of the refinement process reveals whether the generated behavior remains consistent with the learned landscape. This competence signal enables Energy-Gated DAgger, where persistent energy-consistency violations trigger expert takeover and the resulting recovery trajectories are aggregated for subsequent policy updates. EqC integrates naturally into both Diffusion Transformer policies and flow-matching-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies. Across simulation and real-world bimanual manipulation, EqC matches or improves control performance and robustness while enabling timely intervention near the policy's competence boundary. A real-world study further shows how these interventions progressively expand the range of situations handled autonomously, providing a practical path from static generative controllers toward self-improving robot systems.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: Due to practical constraints such as partial observability and limited communication, Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) has become the dominant paradigm in cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). arXiv|arxiv:2610.05476.title: Population Scaling or Data Dilution? Dynamics of Local Topology Evolution in Decentralized Learning
arXiv|arxiv:2610.05476.abstract: Scaling decentralized learning changes not only the number of clients $N$, but also the dynamics of information propagation and consensus. We argue that the effect of increasing $N$ cannot be understood in isolation, because data allocation, topology-dependent mixing, and communication capacity may change simultaneously. We study these coupled effects on CIFAR-10 with $N\in\{10,50,100,200\}$, comparing a degree-two Ring, a Static Random graph, and Local-First Heuristic Evolution (LFHE), a locally adaptive topology process based on friend-of-friend discovery. The Ring provides an analytically transparent failure mode: its Metropolis spectral gap decays as $Θ(N^{-2})$, implying progressively slower contraction of model disagreement as the population grows. Experiments show that holding the nominal local dataset size fixed substantially reduces the apparent population penalty observed when a fixed total dataset is divided among more clients. The remaining degradation depends strongly on communication structure: Ring enters a high-disagreement regime, whereas Static Random and LFHE remain close to consensus. Increasing LFHE's degree threshold further improves accuracy and consensus, but at a substantially higher model-transmission cost. These results show that decentralized scaling is governed by coupled learning and communication dynamics, rather than by the number of clients alone.

arXiv|arxiv:2605.28201.title: Plant, Persist, Trigger: Sleeper Attack on Large Language Model Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2605.28201.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents remain vulnerable to safety threats from the external environment, where attackers inject adversarial content into external observations such as tool-returned data, webpages, or MCP context, causing harmful agentic behaviors such as unsafe actions or incorrect outputs. Existing studies typically focus on single-interaction attacks, where the agent observes adversarial content and immediately exhibits harmful behavior within one user request. However, we show that adversarial content can also persist across interactions served by the same agent, making such threats harder to detect and mitigate. Specifically, adversarial content may persist in the agent state, remain dormant across interactions, and later be activated by a benign user query. We formalize this type of safety threat as Sleeper Attack. To evaluate it, we construct a benchmark with 1,896 instances covering six real-world harmful outcomes, three attack strategies, and three agent state targets: session context, memory, and reusable skills. Experiments on seven strong open-source and closed-source LLMs show that state-of-the-art LLM agents remain vulnerable to Sleeper Attack, even when they achieve low attack success rates under a single-interaction baseline. Our code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/skdvnfu23ihr9wdscnksf1asdffsaef.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.28194.title: HEP-Ex-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Performance in High Energy Physics Experiment Data Analyses with Sealed Worlds
arXiv|arxiv:2611.28194.abstract: Agentic systems are increasingly being explored for automating experimental high-energy physics measurements, but the correctness of their results can today be reliably evaluated only via extensive expert review. To address this, we propose a method to perform detailed quantitative evaluations of agent-driven analyses through the use of blind analysis and injection tests, which are critical in a typical expert review. Agents develop a data analysis pipeline on a public dataset, while the evaluation is performed on programmatically generated sealed private datasets where signals are injected and simulation settings varied within realistic detector uncertainties. By requiring agents to provide a single workflow that is evaluated across these "sealed worlds", we are able to test the accuracy and robustness of the workflows. We demonstrate the approach on four tasks built from CMS open data and present it as a way to reliably benchmark scientific work in experimental high-energy physics. At the time of writing, the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 60% of the score of the expert reference analyses on average, ahead of GPT 6 Astra at 38% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 31%. In individual sessions on one of the tasks, Gemini 4 Argon exceeds the reference. The benchmark is hosted at https://hep-ex-bench.github.io

arXiv|arxiv:2610.28537.title: Beyond 4 bits: Data-Centric Post-training Quantization and Recovery
arXiv|arxiv:2610.28537.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses the weights of a trained model with a limited compute and data budget. Down to 4 bits, state-of-the-art PTQ methods are near-lossless; below this limit, the tested scalar PTQ configurations collapse to near-random accuracy and quality becomes acutely sensitive to choices such as the quantization representation and calibration data. At such low bitwidths, recovery fine-tuning becomes crucial, and its effectiveness depends heavily on these same choices. Yet there is little systematic evidence on how the quantization method, the quality and task alignment of calibration data, and the design of the recovery procedure interact to determine the final 2-bit model. We present a systematic study of 2-bit quantization and recovery fine-tuning across model families, scales, and data distributions, and distill our findings into practical, architecture-dependent best practices for obtaining an accurate 2-bit model. This recipe, which combines a vector codebook representation, a small task-aligned calibration mixture, and a short codebook-only distillation stage, restores 63-68% average accuracy across seven question-answering tasks at 2 bits (a 71-73% BF16 ceiling), versus the near-random 29% of the evaluated scalar PTQ pipelines, at roughly half the compute of a full-model QAT baseline. Given the same calibration and recovery data, EfficientQAT, a trained scalar baseline, avoids the collapse. However, at a matched rate it trails the vector recipe on generation on every model (2.8-10.9 AvgGen; within noise on Qwen3-MoE) and on question answering on three of the four studied models (2.7-7.8 AvgQA). We also find that the best recovery data depends on the calibration data, an interaction confirmed on a held-out model. Our architecture-aware map of the 2-bit design space shows that representation, calibration data, and recovery data must be chosen jointly.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.10942.title: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
arXiv|arxiv:2610.10942.abstract: Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use, under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic's 97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.25689.title: MT-CC: Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Asymmetric Calibration Behavior in Class-Incremental Learning
arXiv|arxiv:2610.25689.abstract: As deep neural networks are required to continuously adapt to evolving data, class-incremental learning (CIL) has become an active research area. However, most existing works primarily focus on improving accuracy while overlooking confidence calibration, which measures the trustworthiness of the model's predictions. Although temperature scaling (TS) is effective for static calibration, it has rarely been explored in continual settings where data distributions evolve over time. In this paper, we introduce Multi-Group Temperature Scaling for Continual Calibration (MT-CC), a novel post-hoc calibration framework that addresses the asymmetric calibration behavior in CIL, where the rate of confidence changes does not align with the rate of accuracy degradation across tasks, leading to different levels of miscalibration. Our key contribution is to design multiple temperature parameters through a lightweight grouping network that separates samples by confidence statistics and task-aware signals in CIL. Furthermore, a Groupwise Difference-between-Confidence-and-Accuracy (GDCA) regularization is incorporated to promote intra-group consistency. Experiments demonstrate that MT-CC significantly improves calibration performance while maintaining accuracy, offering a principled framework for reliable continual learning.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.36722.title: ATTUNER: Recomputation-Free Agentic Context KV Reuse
arXiv|arxiv:2609.36722.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents repeatedly load reusable content, such as skills, documents, and memory entries, into the current context. Re-encoding this content for every request wastes computation. Position-independent caching (PIC) alleviates this by encoding each artifact independently and reusing its key-value (KV) states at arbitrary positions, but it incurs a quality loss relative to full-context prefill. Existing methods repair this loss by restoring global position IDs or recomputing selected tokens. In this work, we isolate the source of the loss, finding that the positional mismatch has minor effect, and independently cached artifacts retain faithful representations: reading a provided artifact stays largely accurate, and performance degrades only when the model must select among multiple artifacts. Moreover, replacing PIC's attention scores with full-prefill scores recovers performance with the cached KV unchanged, localizing the failure to the attention rather than KV recomputation. Motivated by this, we propose \textsc{Attuner}, a query-side adaptation method that learns to read a frozen artifact cache. \textsc{Attuner} inserts low-rank adapters into the query projections and is trained by distilling full-prefill distribution into the student. It trains fewer than 0.05\% of the model parameters and, at inference, requires neither cache recomputation nor a full-context reference. On Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B across seven benchmarks covering skills, documents, memory, and code, \textsc{Attuner} substantially outperforms prior PIC baselines in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, matches full-context prefill quality while providing up to $3.73\times$ speedup.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.37398.title: An end-to-end framework for uncertainty-aware validation of generative models
arXiv|arxiv:2610.37398.abstract: Density estimation with generative models is a common task in the physical sciences, for example in background estimation in particle physics. Existing machine learning techniques, however, lack methods to quantify uncertainties that can be propagated into a statistical test. That limits the validation of generative models to standard goodness-of-fit tests, in which the generative model is treated as exact (point-null hypothesis). But a model fitted to a finite training set is never exact, so if its uncertainties are neglected, any sufficiently powerful goodness-of-fit test will eventually reject it once the test set is large enough to resolve this estimation error. We propose SIGMA, an end-to-end framework combining density estimation with principled uncertainty quantification. We use Gaussian mixture models, for which uncertainties are tractable, and further construct a new goodness-of-fit test in which these uncertainties are profiled as nuisance parameters to account for the statistical error of the fit, promoting the conventional point-null test to a composite one. A rejection then signals genuine mismodeling rather than a test set large enough to resolve the error of the fit, provided the propagated uncertainties faithfully cover that error. We demonstrate the framework on a controlled two-dimensional toy model and on a collider physics benchmark modeling the QCD background process. With uncertainties included, the same model can be trusted on test sets up to an order of magnitude larger than the standard test allows. Our work thus provides a statistically grounded basis for a robust use of generative models in the physical sciences.

arXiv|arxiv:2406.13144.title: GroupChat-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Term Understanding of Realistic Group Chats
arXiv|arxiv:2406.13144.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to participate in persistent group communication, yet existing dialogue benchmarks largely focus on short, dyadic, or single-session interactions. We introduce GroupChat-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating long-term understanding in scripted multi-party dialogues that serve as a proxy for group chats. Built from TV show scripts to avoid privacy concerns, each conversation stream spans five consecutive seasons and approximately 1,300 sessions. The benchmark tests whether agents can track participant-specific information, interpersonal relationships, and contextual changes over time. Its question pools combine refined fan-quiz-style questions with template-based questions generated from temporal knowledge graphs. Agents are evaluated as dialogue sessions unfold chronologically, with access only to the conversation history available when each question is posed. To probe the influence of memorized knowledge, GroupChat-Bench includes unanswerable questions and settings with new or swapped character names. We also propose GroupChat-Mem, which combines structured memory with a raw session repository. Experiments reveal limitations in existing memory systems, while GroupChat-Mem provides a stronger baseline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/jwyang21/groupchat_bench/.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.15810.title: Adaptive Look, Flexible Thought: Learning How and How Long to Think in Multimodal Reasoning
arXiv|arxiv:2610.15810.abstract: The introduction of long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and external tools has substantially improved the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on general and reasoning tasks. However, existing fast-slow reasoning paradigms mainly regulate textual reasoning length, while visual computation introduced by external tools or visual tokens is often treated as an auxiliary component. This separation prevents MLLMs from jointly optimizing visual perception and textual reasoning. To address this issue, we propose L2T (adaptive Look, flexible Thought), a unified reasoning framework that jointly optimizes the form and depth of computation. L2T first discretizes tool-produced visual states into visual tokens, bringing visual perception and textual reasoning into a shared autoregressive space. Based on this unified representation, L2T introduces a modality-aware routing reward to select appropriate reasoning modes and a difficulty-aware fast-slow strategy to adapt reasoning depth according to task complexity. Experiments on general perception and reasoning-intensive tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of L2T. Compared with explicit tool-calling approaches, L2T maintains competitive performance while achieving 1.7--3.6 times higher throughput.
